inline.s: When the wild, deluded mind turns with the impulses of feeling (acting along with karma), then at the time of death one is dragged along by karma.
Once one follows deluded thoughts
one does whatever one wishes to do, without using the wisdom that awakens to principle to choose between right and wrong, benefit and harm, like a drunkard or a madman
and so at the time of death one is
dragged
along
by karma
and receives the corresponding future retribution.
When awake, one is not carried away by feeling
and at death one can transform karma
When the mind is awake and does not turn with the impulses of feeling (going against karma), then at the time of death one can transform karma (karma cannot bind one).

When feeling wants to do something, but one examines the principle and sees that it should not be done, one must stop at once. When feeling does not want to do something, but one reflects on principle and sees that it should be done, one must go and do it at once. Simply follow the principle of right and wrong, and do not follow the feelings of like and dislike; then at the time of death karma cannot bind you, and even though the intermediate state comes, you go wherever you wish, taking birth freely among the heavens and among humans.

In short, whatever one does from morning to night, if one is dragged along by the impulses of feeling, then at the time of death one is dragged along by karma and receives rebirth according to karma: good karma brings birth in a good realm, evil karma brings birth in an evil realm. But if whatever one does is based on awakened wisdom and not on the impulses of feeling, then at the time of death it is up to oneself, and one goes wherever one wishes. If you want to test where you will go at the time of death, whether you will be master of yourself or not, you need only examine your ordinary way of using the mind: in the face of sense objects, are you free or not free?

Therefore, in ordinary times one must train in the skill of “awakened awareness turning the thought.” One must be sharply awake at all times, and train this mind until it can rein in the horse at the edge of the cliff, stopping when it is time to stop and letting go when it is time to let go. One must be quick to notice and quick to turn, so that burning affliction at once becomes a place of coolness. On this point, Master Hanshan, in his Dream Roamings: Reply to General Yang Yuanru, gives a penetrating instruction, which is annotated below:

[The ancients said: ‘In the field of fevered confusion, it is hard to withstand a cool eye.’ For the three realms are without peace, like a burning house, and none who come and go within them are not cooked and scorched by it. If one would find a patch of cool ground amid the blazing flames, none but a person with a cool eye can obtain it. If one can make the present thought cool, one suddenly sees the whole earth turned to ice, and naturally one no longer takes the world of body and mind as a place of refuge. This is how, from of old, people of great strength play in the field of birth and death, able to turn dusty toil into Buddha-work and transform affliction into bodhi — it rests solely on that one cool eye and that one cool-heartedness of theirs. What other miraculous powers and wondrous functions could there be?]

The ancients said: ‘In the field of fevered confusion, though everything churns the mind, still it cannot withstand being looked upon with a cool eye.’ Because the three realms are without peace, like a burning house, none who come and go within them are not cooked and scorched. If one would find a patch of cool ground amid the blazing flames, only a person with a cool eye can manage it. If one looks upon the world with a cool eye, and looks until the present thought is cool, then one suddenly sees the whole earth turned to ice, and naturally one will not take the world of body and mind as a refuge. Since ancient times, people of great strength who play in the field of birth and death, able to turn dusty toil into Buddha-work and transform affliction into bodhi, rely precisely on that one cool eye and that one cool-heartedness of theirs — what other miraculous powers and wondrous functions could there be?

[The three realms are without peace, like a burning house] The Lotus Sutra says: “The three realms are without peace, like a burning house, filled with many sufferings, greatly to be feared; there are always the sorrows of birth, aging, sickness, and death; such fires blaze without cease.” [It rests solely on that one cool eye and that one cool-heartedness of theirs] This means: when the mind is empty, the objects are empty of themselves; the ten thousand dharmas bind nothing and are originally liberated. The Diamond Sutra says: “All that has marks is false and delusive.” “Not grasping at marks, one dwells unmoving, as thus.” Of these two lines of scripture, “All that has marks is false and delusive” — this is the cool eye; “Not grasping at marks, one dwells unmoving, as thus” — this is the cool-heartedness. In this passage, “qu” (that one) means “his” or “her.”

[These words are very easy to know, and very hard to see. Take, for instance, how the Buddhas and patriarchs make the single saying ‘all dharmas are like a dream’ the essential road of world-transcendence. Yet the wise and the foolish of the world can all alike say that life is a dream. Their words may seem the same, but their meaning is not. In truth they have never truly, with one glance, seen through life as a dream. If one had truly seen through it, then naturally at every pass of honor and disgrace, profit and harm, gain and loss, right and wrong, one would swing one’s arms and walk away — and who would dare stand against one’s edge?]

These words (‘In the field of fevered confusion, it is hard to withstand a cool eye’) are very easy to know, yet their true meaning is very hard to see. It is just as when the Buddhas and patriarchs make the single saying ‘all dharmas are like a dream’ the essential road of world-transcendence — but how many people see its true meaning? The wise and the foolish of the world all alike can say ‘life is a dream.’ It is the same phrase, ‘life is a dream,’ yet the flavor of that phrase in the mouth of the wise and in the mouth of the foolish is wholly different. The foolish man may say it with his lips, but in truth he has never truly, with one glance, seen through life as a dream. If one had truly seen through it, then naturally at every pass of honor and disgrace, profit and harm, gain and loss, right and wrong, one could turn and walk away — and who could hold one back? (The carp slips off the golden hook and is gone, wagging head and tail, never to return.)
[Swing one’s arms] To swing the arms and walk off — to leave without a backward glance.

[In truth there is nothing very mysterious in it. As for the first step, however, it does have its method. In dealing with the world, one should first take the matters of this dream and hold them up before one’s eyes, observing them closely. One must see them truly and distinctly, until one cannot help but burst into a great laugh. At that point, one suddenly feels that the ordinary saying ‘like a dream’ is utterly different from before. Then, taking this very place of laughter, in a single thought turn the present circumstances around and place them within the dream, observing them closely. When one sees them hazy and heavy, upside down and topsy-turvy, one suddenly gives a sharp start and wakes. In this way, looking back upon one’s life, all the various circumstances one has passed through — seek them truly, and they cannot be found. This place where they cannot be found is the first gate through which all Buddhas and patriarchs pass beyond birth and death.]

In truth there is nothing very mysterious in it. As for taking the first step, it does have its own method. The method is this: in dealing with the world, one should first take the matters of this dream and hold them up before one’s eyes, observing them closely. One must look truly and distinctly, until one cannot help but laugh aloud. At that point, one suddenly feels that the ordinary saying ‘life is a dream’ carries a wholly different flavor. Then, taking this place of laughter and awakening, in a single thought turn it toward the present circumstances and place them within the frame of ‘life is a dream,’ observing them closely. When one sees oneself hazy and muddled, upside down and topsy-turvy, one suddenly gives a sharp start and wakes. In this way, looking back upon one’s life, all the various circumstances one has passed through — even if one wanted to take them as real, they cannot be found (one simply cannot manage it). This place where they cannot be found is the first gate through which all Buddhas and patriarchs pass beyond birth and death.

[The place where one cannot help but burst into a great laugh] Master Hanshan’s Song of Awakening the World says: “Alive, in vain you spend a thousand, ten thousand thoughts; in death, you leave behind but empty hands. Joy and sorrow, parting and meeting — clamor day after day; long life or early death, poverty or success — busy day after day. Do not strive to be strong and fight for victory: a hundred years are all a stage of play. In a moment the gong and drum fall silent — and who knows where your homeland lies?”
Question: Who is wild and deluded? Who is it that at the time of death is dragged along by karma? Who is awake? Who is it that at the time of death karma cannot bind?

Answer: The self-nature is wild and deluded. It is the self-nature that at the time of death is dragged along by karma; it is the self-nature that follows karma and receives rebirth. The self-nature is awake. It is the self-nature that at the time of death karma cannot bind; it is the self-nature that goes wherever it wishes.

Question: Master Guifeng set forth three levels: subduing affliction, cutting off affliction, and perfectly realizing the fruit of Buddhahood. Why does this chapter take as its title only “not bound by karma,” which belongs to the subduing of affliction?

Answer: To cut off affliction in this very life, and even to perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood, is very good indeed. But those who can do so are as rare as phoenix feathers and unicorn horns, and all of them laid the foundation in former lives.
And to accomplish “at the time of death, karma cannot bind one, and one goes wherever one wishes,”
no prior foundation is needed

. As long as in this life one cultivates correctly and with diligent effort, anyone may attain in this very life the state in which “whenever deluded thoughts arise, one does not follow them,” and therefore “at the time of death, karma cannot bind one, and one goes wherever one wishes.”

In this way, not only will one avoid “suffering the pains of the evil realms, bobbing up and down in the vast sea of karma without knowing in which life one can again study the Buddhadharma”; one may also be born at will in the pure lands of the Buddhas. Moreover, having already subdued affliction in this life, one lays a good foundation for continuing cultivation in the next, and does not suffer the three-life wrong. With such profit of three gains in one stroke,
“not bound by karma” should be the goal for which the broad community of Chan practitioners strives in this life
, and so this chapter takes it as its title.

[The three-life wrong] Because one cultivates in this life, in the next life one enjoys the reward of blessings, and then, relying on those blessings, one commits evil, which brings about a further fall in the life after that. Even when the karma of hell is exhausted, one is reborn again as a hungry ghost or an animal, and to regain human form becomes difficult beyond difficulty. That is why the World-Honored One asked Ānanda, holding up a bit of earth in his hand: “Is the earth in my hand more, or the earth of the great ground more?” Ānanda answered: “The earth of the great ground is more.” The Buddha said: “Those who gain human form are like the earth in my hand; those who lose human form are like the earth of the great ground.” Hence, “through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lives, no one to rely on or turn to”!
Question: What should one do when temptation attacks?

Answer: There is a saying: “If temptation attacks you with cruel force, overcome it with reasonable analysis and an unyielding will — every desire can be mastered.” — The cool eye, the cool heart; seeing through, letting go. Therefore, when temptation attacks, immediately raise the illumination of wisdom: when the deviant comes, save it with the right; when the deluded come, save them with the awakened; when the foolish come, save them with wisdom; when the evil come, save them with goodness. Overcome temptation with penetrating principle and firm will. The skill must be practiced constantly, constantly reflected upon and summed up, going deeper and deeper, until inwardly one does not turn with thoughts and outwardly one is not dragged by objects.
About
“whenever deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them, and then at the time of death karma naturally cannot bind one”
, Elder Yuanyin said:

“This brings us to the time of death — what happens then? To be free in taking birth at the time of death, one must in ordinary times do the work of ‘whenever deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them.’ If our deluded thoughts are not yet completely cut off, and in a single instant a deluded thought comes again, we must immediately become aware of it and not run after it. If the deluded thought is strong and we are aware of it but cannot cut it off, then quickly recite the Buddha’s name, recite a mantra, or take up the huatou and ask where this deluded thought comes from, thus dissolving the deluded thought. If we have run a long way after the deluded thought before we realize it, then it is already too late. How quickly one becomes aware and how fast one cuts off is a matter of the strength of one’s practice. It is like the difference in brightness between a candle flame and an electric light. At first one can illumine, but later one cannot see much; only long after a deluded thought has arisen does one know it — that is a candle flame. When the practice has become pure and ripe, a thought has but to arise and one can illumine it at once, as a strong electric light shines before one, so that every pit and hollow can be seen clearly; walking the night road, one will not fall into a pit or a ditch — this is the electric light. This is to reach the stage of ‘quiescent yet ever illumining, illumining yet ever quiescent’; one need not intend to illumine, for one illumines naturally. The skill in this differs greatly in depth. In doing the work we must be aware at all times and practice densely and continuously. If out of twenty-four hours a day one practices for only one or two hours, and does not practice for the other twenty-two, that is far too slack, and it will be very hard to make progress. Therefore in the four deportments of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, we must practice at all times and be aware at all times, so that the practice can advance. Furthermore, when deluded thoughts arise, do not follow after ‘any’ of them. Do not think that some deluded thought is a good one and so follow after it. Someone has a good dream, and after waking cannot bear to let it go, still thinking about it. The dream is false to begin with — why be attached to it? In a dream you became emperor — are you really an emperor? In a dream you got a great treasure — did you really get the treasure? To cling to it — is that not foolish? People are just this foolish! Chan Master Guifeng, with earnest painstaking care, tells us: ‘whenever deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them’ — do not run after them. If we truly accomplish this, then ‘at the time of death, karma cannot bind one.’ To bind means to tie up. All sentient beings run after karma! Those with good karma ascend to the heavens; those with evil karma descend into hell. If one can truly keep from running after deluded thoughts when they arise, then at that time karma cannot tie you up, and you can be free.”
(A Brief Commentary on the Great Seal)

blocks.text: Chapter 6: Equal Holding of Samādhi and Prajñā

inline.s: Prajñā: All that has marks is false and delusive.
Samādhi: Not grasping at marks
one dwells unmoving, as thus.
Samādhi and prajñā held equally.
Do not fear impermanence,
dissolution and collapse are the prelude to new birth,
follow along without resisting,
the seal breaks and the pattern is formed.
[The four marks] The mark of self, the mark of others, the mark of sentient beings, the mark of a life span. (For details see
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
) [The seal
breaks
and the pattern (
the flowered design

) is formed] A wax seal carved with a pattern is pressed onto a clay mold. When the clay mold is heated and dried, the wax seal melts, and the pattern imprinted on the clay mold is formed. This is a metaphor for using the physical body to cultivate so as to
accomplish the work of the Way:
when the breath stops, though the physical body dies (the seal breaks), yet
the great matter of ending birth and death
is accomplished in that very moment (the pattern is formed).
The Collection of the Blissful Land says:
“As when a wax seal is pressed on clay, the seal breaks and the pattern is formed; when this life is cut off, that is the time of birth in the Land of Bliss
(that is, the time of rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
[Clay mold] A mold used for casting metal vessels.
When Śākyamuni Buddha, seated beneath the bodhi tree, saw the morning star at dawn and awakened to the Way, he said:
“How wondrous! How wondrous! All sentient beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue, but because of deluded thinking and attachment they cannot realize it.”

Therefore cultivation is simply the removing of deluded thinking and attachment. Remove deluded thinking and attachment, and one realizes one’s own Tathāgata wisdom and virtue — one is a Buddha; otherwise one is a sentient being.

When the mind is not scattered and deluded thoughts are extinguished, this is samādhi; when one lets go of attachment to the ten thousand dharmas and is not confused by illusory marks into discrimination and calculation, liking and disliking, taking and rejecting, this is prajñā. Luminous awareness extinguishing deluded thoughts — this is samādhi; the patience of wisdom letting go of attachment — this is prajñā. To hold samādhi and prajñā equally is to cultivate and apply luminous awareness and the patience of wisdom together, in tandem.
Luminous awareness: perfectly clear and distinct, yet without thought and without recollection. In the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury, the Buddha says:
“The anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi of all Buddhas is entirely without thought and without recollection.”
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
“What is meant by enlightenment is that the essence of the mind is free from recollection.”
The Essentials of the Transmission of the Mind says:
“Just as you are, it is; stir a thought and you miss it.” “Still the recollection and forget the reckoning, and the Buddha appears of himself.”
Chan Master Da’an says:
“If you
(all of you)

wish to become Buddhas, simply be without all those topsy-turvy clingings and seekings, deluded thoughts and evil perceptions, and the defiled, desirous, impure mind of a sentient being — then you are Buddhas of initial resolve and right awakening”
(Records of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era)
Luminous awareness has three levels: awakened illumination, quiescent illumination, and perfect illumination.
1. “Awakened illumination”: using the awakened mind to illumine all things, so that coarse thoughts come to rest.
2. “Quiescent illumination”: the mind is quiescent yet illumines, so that subtle thoughts come to rest. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“When purity is complete, the light penetrates everywhere; quiescent illumination encompasses empty space.”
The Zhengchen Lun says:
“True suchness illumining yet eternally quiescent is dharma-nature; quiescent yet eternally illumining is dharmakāya. Though in meaning there are two names, quiescence and illumination are not two.”
3. “Perfect illumination”: the illumination of wondrous enlightenment, so that the subtlest thoughts come to rest. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All Tathāgatas, in the ground of their initial resolve, rely on the pure, enlightening mark of perfect illumination to cut off ignorance forever, and only then accomplish the Buddha Way.”
It also says:
“Birth and death and nirvana are the same as arising and ceasing. Wondrous enlightenment’s perfect illumination is free from the flower in the sky and the film over the eye
(free from the flower in empty space and the delusive film)
(For annotation see
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

The patience of wisdom: cultivating the practice of patience in order to escape birth and death and perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. This has two aspects: the patience of acceptance and the patience of serene acceptance. The patience of acceptance is to endure adverse conditions without giving rise to anger; the patience of serene acceptance is to abide peacefully in the present moment without the mind moving — that is, to accept, to follow along with, to surrender to the present moment. Master Hanshan says:
“The single practice of patience is the foremost wondrous practice for attaining Buddhahood.”
(Dream Roamings
Instruction to the Chan Practitioner Fajin)
The patience of acceptance: when words are adverse, one can bear them; when affairs go against one, one can remain at peace; hunger and cold one can endure; when desire arises, one can purify it.
[Hunger and cold one can endure] The body’s fatigue, discomfort, misery, and sickness can all be endured; here hunger and cold stand for them all.
The patience of serene acceptance: to accept the present moment, to surrender to the present moment, not grasping at marks, with the patient mind unmoving.
In the Diamond Sutra, the Buddha says:
“All that has marks is false and delusive.”
It also says:
“Not grasping at marks, one dwells unmoving, as thus.”
(For annotation see
A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra
On surrendering to the present moment, Eckhart
Tolle’s
The Power of Now
offers a fine exposition. For example, he writes:

“Most human suffering is unnecessary. It is self-created, because an unobserved mind is running your life. The pain you create now always comes from some form of non-acceptance, some form of unconscious resistance to what is. On the level of thought, the resistance is some form of judgment. On the level of emotion, it is some form of negativity. The intensity of the pain depends on the degree of resistance to the present moment, and this in turn depends on how strongly you are identified with your mind, for the mind always seeks to deny the Now and to escape from it. In other words, the more you are identified with your mind, the more you suffer. Or you may put it like this: the more you are able to honor and accept the Now, the more you are free of pain, of suffering — and free of the egoic mind.”
“Nonresistance to the flow of life is to live in a state of grace, ease, and lightness. This state is then no longer dependent upon things being in a certain way, good or bad.”

“When you surrender to what is and so become fully present, the past ceases to have any power. You do not need it anymore. Presence is the key. Now, the realm of Being, which has been obscured by the mind, is revealed. Suddenly, there is a great stillness within you — an unfathomable sense of peace. In that peace there is great joy. In that joy there is love. And at the very core of it all is the sacred, the immeasurable, the unnameable ‘
That
’ which is.

“All negativity (from irritation and impatience to furious rage, from a depressed mood and sullen resentment to suicidal despair) is resistance. Whenever negativity arises, treat it as a signal to remind yourself: surrender, and be more present.”

Surrender is perfectly compatible with taking action, making changes, or achieving goals. But in the surrendered state a totally different quality of energy flows into what you do. Surrender reconnects you with the energy source of Being, and if your action is infused with Being, it becomes a celebration of life energy that takes you deeper into the Now.

Through nonresistance, the quality of your consciousness is greatly enhanced, and the quality of whatever you do is bound to change as well. Then good results naturally appear and reflect that quality. We may call this ‘action in surrender.’
In the state of surrender you can see clearly what needs to be done, and then you take action, doing one thing at a time and focusing on one thing at a time.
Learn from nature: see how all things complete their actions naturally, and how life unfolds its miracles without any dissatisfaction or displeasure.”
“If you can take no action at this moment, and cannot withdraw from the situation either, then use the situation to make you go deeper into surrender, deeper into the Now, deeper into Being.

“When you enter the timeless dimension of presence, change may come about in unexpected ways, without your having to expend much effort. Life will offer its aid, and be very cooperative. If inner factors such as fear, guilt, or laziness prevent you from taking action, they too will dissolve in the light of your conscious presence.”
The patience of wisdom has four levels: the patience of initial acquiescence, the patience of gentle compliance, the patience of non-arising, and the patience of quiescent cessation.

1. “The patience of initial acquiescence”: the practitioner of initial resolve, amid favorable and adverse conditions, endures by taming and subduing the mind, accomplishing “not grasping at marks, dwelling unmoving, as thus.”

2. “The patience of gentle compliance”: having tamed and subdued the mind for a long time, when meeting conditions and circumstances one need not force restraint, but can be patient naturally, accomplishing “not grasping at marks, dwelling unmoving, as thus.” At this point the mind is gentle, good, and compliant.

3. “The patience of non-arising”: one who has entered the noble stages realizes that all dharmas are originally non-arising; sentient and insentient alike are produced by conditions and have no fixed nature, and are empty just as they are. Therefore, within the dharma of no-nature, the patient mind does not move, and one personally realizes non-arising.
[No-nature] Nature means essence; since all dharmas have no substantial essence, this is called no-nature (illusion). The Lotus Sutra says:
“Know that all dharmas are ever without nature.”
The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“All illusions become no-nature.”

4. “The patience of quiescent cessation”: the sage at the stage of fruition, who has thoroughly realized the quiescent realm of nirvana, in both the marks of movement and of stillness accords with thusness.

[Thusness] The realm of self-nature in which upside-down discrimination does not arise. Because it is the true suchness (the true mark of all dharmas) realized by the wisdom of thusness, it is called “thusness.”

Luminous awareness and the patience of wisdom complement and complete each other. Luminous awareness is the pillar of the sea that steadies the patience of wisdom, and the patience of wisdom is an essential precondition for luminous awareness. For luminous awareness to be continuous, lasting, and resistant to disturbance, besides strengthening the cultivation of awareness, the cultivation of the patience of wisdom is also very important. A small impatience ruins a great plan; lose luminous awareness, and you lose liberation.

One must make up one’s mind to perform surgery on oneself. This visible world is illusory, like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; it is impermanent, like lightning or a spark struck from stone; it is a cage woven by yourself. When you no longer identify with this visible world, no longer take it as real, permanent, and bound up with your own weal and woe, but step outside it as an outsider, then you (the self-nature) are liberated from this visible world, and the suffering you created yourself comes to an end. You may still take part in the creation of this visible world, but you will not be attached to results, nor be abused and tormented by it; instead you walk your own road freely and as your own master.
Master Hanshan says:

“If you cannot peacefully endure and are obstructed by affliction, then the moment you see it arising, take up the Sixth Patriarch’s line ‘originally there is not a single thing,’ and it will be like the sword of a king of adamant: all affliction will at once melt like ice, and body and mind will be transformed into a cool pool.”

[Originally there is not a single thing] All things are illusory and have never existed. The Sixth Patriarch’s verse says: “Bodhi fundamentally has no tree, nor does the bright mirror have a stand. Originally there is not a single thing — where could dust ever cling?” (For annotation see
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

Only the patience of wisdom can wear away the mark of self, the mark of others, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of a life span; as it is said, “hardship and bitter toil complete you like jade.” The important methods for cultivating patience are: in ordinary times, do much self-reflection; when facing circumstances, always raise the illumination of wisdom — when the deviant come, save them with the right; when the deluded come, save them with the awakened; when the foolish come, save them with wisdom; when the evil come, save them with goodness.
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:

“Believing in one’s own nature, knowing that the mind moves deludedly and that no objects truly lie before it, one cultivates the practice of detachment. Because one knows in accordance with reality that no objects lie before one, one employs various skillful means and undertakes practices of compliance, neither grasping nor recollecting. And so, through the power of long-continued permeation, ignorance is extinguished. Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind no longer arises. Because there is no arising, objects cease accordingly. Because both cause and condition cease together, the marks of mind all come to an end, and this is called attaining nirvana.”

Translation: Believe that the self-nature is originally pure and undefiled; know that all the myriad appearances are merely various illusory marks manifested by the deluded movement of one’s own mind, and that in reality no such objects exist; therefore cultivate the practice of detachment (knowing illusion, one is at once detached). Because one knows in accordance with reality that no objects lie before one, one employs various skillful means and undertakes practices of compliance, neither grasping nor recollecting. And so, through long-continued permeation in this way, ignorance is extinguished. Because ignorance is extinguished, the mind no longer moves deludedly. Because it no longer moves deludedly, the objects before one cease accordingly. Because the causes and conditions of aversion and longing cease together, the marks of mind are utterly extinguished, and this is called attaining nirvana.

[The practice of detachment] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing illusion, one is at once detached, without employing skillful means; detaching from illusion, one is at once enlightened, and there are no gradual stages.” [Because cause and condition cease together] The earlier text says: “Because this deluded mind has the causes and conditions of aversion and longing, it permeates true suchness.”
Master Hanshan says:

“One who does not train and temper himself amid conditions and circumstances is only dealing with matters at the gate of light and shadow; and when faced with the eight winds of favorable and adverse circumstances, he will be shaken and snatched away, unable to pass through them at all.”
(Dream Roamings
Miscellaneous Words from Mount Jing)

[The gate of light and shadow] This means that one’s seeing of the Way is not genuine. The bright moon in the sky stands for the Way; the moon’s reflection in water stands for where the Way flows forth. One should look up from the reflection to the moon in the sky, and should not take the moon’s reflection in water for the true moon. [The eight winds] “The eight winds” are the eight favorable and adverse circumstances: gain, loss, defamation, eulogy, praise, ridicule, sorrow, and joy. “Gain” is to obtain advancement and success; “loss” is to suffer damage and retreat. “Defamation” is to be slandered behind one’s back; “eulogy” is to be praised behind one’s back. “Praise” is to be praised to one’s face; “ridicule” is to be mocked to one’s face. “Sorrow” is the various pains of body and mind; “joy” is the various pleasures of body and mind. These eight dharmas are always loved or hated by worldly people, and can moreover stir the human heart, and so they are likened to “the eight winds.”
Question: How can one eliminate self-attachment and become free of the four marks (the mark of self, the mark of others, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of a life span)?

Answer: Self-attachment shows itself in resistance to the present moment, in judgment, in liking and disliking, in taking and rejecting. The best way to let go of self-attachment and escape the ego’s control is to cultivate the patience of wisdom, accomplishing in turn the patience of initial acquiescence and the patience of gentle compliance. If one accomplishes the patience of non-arising, then attachment to dharmas is eliminated as well.
As to why one should cultivate patience and how to cultivate it, Master Hanshan gives a penetrating instruction in his Dream Roamings

Instruction to the Chan Practitioner Fajin. This instruction carries great power to gather and move the reader, and it is to be hoped that practitioners will ponder it again and again and put it into practice again and again. It is annotated below:

[Fajin said of himself that his nature had a strong habit of anger, and so the old man, using skillful means to tame and subdue him, taught him the Dharma gate of patience. He further instructed him, saying: Great Master Yongjia has said: My teacher saw the Buddha Burning Lamp, and for many kalpas was a sage of patience. From this we know that the single practice of patience is the foremost wondrous practice for attaining Buddhahood.]

Fajin said of himself that the habit of anger was very strong, so the old man (Hanshan’s own designation for himself) used skillful means to tame and subdue him, and taught him the Dharma gate of patience. He further instructed him, saying that Great Master Yongjia’s Song of Realizing the Way says: “My teacher saw the Buddha Burning Lamp, and for many kalpas was a sage of patience.” From this we know that the single practice of “patience” is the foremost wondrous practice for attaining Buddhahood.

[Therefore my teacher, Śākyamuni, life after life and birth after birth, was slandered and harmed by Devadatta, even to the present life. Every kind of dharma-destroying act, nothing left undone, and even killers of his life more than once. Yet at the Lotus assembly he bestowed on him the prediction of Buddhahood, and said: My thirty-two marks and eighty excellent characteristics, my supreme and wondrous virtues, were all accomplished because of the good friend Devadatta. Is this not to say that the single practice of patience is the essential practice for attaining Buddhahood? He also said: Formerly, when King Kali cut my body apart, at that time I had no mark of self, no mark of others, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a life span; if I had had the mark of self, the mark of others, the mark of sentient beings, or the mark of a life span, the Buddha Burning Lamp would not have given me the prediction.]

Therefore our World-Honored One, life after life and birth after birth, was slandered and harmed by Devadatta, down to this present life. Devadatta’s various dharma-destroying acts left nothing undone, and he even tried to kill the World-Honored One more than once. Yet at the Lotus assembly the World-Honored One bestowed on him the prediction of Buddhahood, and said: The reason I have realized the thirty-two marks and eighty excellent characteristics, and supreme and wondrous virtues, is that they were all accomplished through the persecution of the good friend Devadatta. Is this not to say that the single practice of “patience” is the essential practice for attaining Buddhahood? The World-Honored One also says in the Diamond Sutra: In former times I was cut apart by King Kali, and at that time I had no mark of self, no mark of others, no mark of sentient beings, no mark of a life span; if I had had the mark of self, the mark of others, the mark of sentient beings, or the mark of a life span, the Buddha Burning Lamp would not have given me the prediction.

[Devadatta] The Buddha’s cousin, who left home and studied miraculous powers; his body possessed thirty marks, and he repeatedly persecuted the Buddha. [My teacher saw the Buddha Burning Lamp, and for many kalpas was a sage of patience] That the World-Honored One (my teacher) met the Buddha Burning Lamp and received the prediction of Buddhahood was entirely due to the tempering of having been a sage of patience for many kalpas. Wholly contrary to worldly people, the Buddha takes being insulted as a good thing, for only through a hundred refinings does one become steel, and only through patience can one wear away the mark of self, the mark of others, the mark of sentient beings, and the mark of a life span; as it is said, “hardship and bitter toil complete you like jade.” [Saw the Buddha Burning Lamp] In former times, when the World-Honored One was a bodhisattva of the seventh ground, he met the Buddha Burning Lamp and heard the Dharma, realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, and ascended to the eighth ground; the Buddha Burning Lamp then gave him the prediction, saying: After ninety-one kalpas, in the kalpa named Worthy, you shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Śākyamuni. [Prediction] A Buddha’s beforehand recording of a bodhisattva’s name: after how many ages, in such and such a place and land, he will become what Buddha. [The Worthy Kalpa] The past great kalpa is called the Adorned Kalpa, the future great kalpa is called the Star Constellation Kalpa, and the Worthy Kalpa is the present great kalpa; because in this great kalpa a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, it is called the “Worthy Kalpa.”

[For all sentient beings, the whole mass of birth, death, and suffering comes into being through having a self; the supreme bodhi, the adornment of merit and wisdom, is arrived at through having no self. Because self is set in opposition to things, right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, liking and disliking are established; liking and disliking established, joy and anger proliferate; the self-nature grows turbid and the mind-ground grows dim; the mind-ground dim, all evils grow; all evils growing, all sufferings gather; all sufferings gathering, birth and death are prolonged! All of this is brought about by the self. How grievous is the harm done by the self! It is like a heavily fortified city with elite troops — how could it easily be broken?]

The reason all sentient beings have birth, death, and suffering is that these are established through having a self; the supreme bodhi, the adornment of merit and wisdom, is realized through having no self. When the self is taken as the center, one stands in opposition to others, and so right and wrong arise; right and wrong arising, liking and disliking are established; liking and disliking established, joy and anger proliferate. And so the self-nature grows turbid and the mind-ground grows dim; the mind-ground dim, all evils grow; all evils growing, all sufferings gather; all sufferings gathering, birth and death and the round of rebirth never end! All of this is brought about by having a “self.” How grievous is the harm done by the self! Yet to break self-attachment is like attacking a fortress closely guarded by elite troops — how could it be easily broken!

[Having a self] To take the physical body (the four great elements) as one’s own body, and thoughts (the illusory reflections of the six dusts) as one’s own mind. [No self] Not to take the physical body (the four great elements) as one’s own body, nor thoughts (the illusory reflections of the six dusts) as one’s own mind, but rather to take the dharmakāya as one’s own body and spiritual knowing as one’s own mind. [Setting the self in opposition to things] To take the self as the center and stand in opposition to others. Here “things” means people other than oneself.

[Laozi has said: The soft overcomes the hard, the weak overcomes the strong. This is the initial stage of the practice of patience. Sentient beings rely on their self-view, which is firm and hard to break; therefore a single word against them cannot be borne, a single affair gone contrary cannot be accepted, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified — all of this is not knowing the method of patience, and merely increasing the attachment of self-view! Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the practice of harmony. He also said: The forbearance of the dharma of suffering, the wisdom of the dharma of suffering. He also said: The patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is attained only at the eighth ground. From this we know that, from the forbearance of the arising of dharmas, enduring on to non-arising, the wondrous practice is perfected and the fruit of Buddhahood accomplished! The single practice of patience — how could it be shallow! Therefore it is said: In whatever you do, you should practice patience.]

Laozi’s Daode Jing says: “The soft overcomes the hard, the weak overcomes the strong.” This is the initial stage of the practice of patience. The self-view that sentient beings hold is firm and hard to break, and so a single word against them cannot be borne, a single affair gone contrary cannot be accepted, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified — all of this is not knowing the method of patience, and merely ceaselessly strengthening the attachment to self-view! Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to cultivate the practice of harmony. He also said: “The forbearance of the dharma of suffering, the wisdom of the dharma of suffering.” He also said: “The patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is attained only by a bodhisattva of the eighth ground.” From this we know that, from the forbearance of the arising of dharmas, enduring all the way until nirvana (non-arising) is accomplished, the wondrous practice is perfected and the fruit of Buddhahood accomplished! The single practice of “patience” — how could it be a trifling matter! Therefore it is said: In whatever you do, you must be able to practice patience.

[Self-view] Also called self-attachment. The deluded clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates as oneself. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have all kinds of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another (for example, taking east as west, south as north, and so on), deludedly taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the illusory reflections of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like one with a diseased eye who sees flowers in empty space and a second moon. Good man! In empty space there are truly no flowers; the diseased one deludedly clings to them. Because of deluded clinging, he is not only confused about the self-nature of this empty space, but also deluded about the place where the real flowers arise. From this delusion comes the turning round in birth and death, and so it is called ignorance.” [The four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, wind has movement as its nature. All material forms in the world possess these four natures of hardness, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called “great.” [The illusory reflections of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six sense faculties come into contact with the six dusts; and since these thoughts are illusory and unreal, they are called the illusory reflections of the six dusts — the illusory shadows conditioned by the six dusts.

[A single word against them cannot be borne, a single affair gone contrary cannot be accepted, a single hunger or cold cannot be endured, a single thought of desire cannot be purified] This speaks of those who cannot be patient. Patience means being able to accomplish this: when words are adverse, one can bear them; when affairs go against one, one can remain at peace; hunger and cold one can endure; when desire arises, one can purify it. [Harmony] Harmony has the harmony of principle and the harmony of affairs. The harmony of principle is the realization of cessation by choice, that is, everyone together cultivating and realizing this commonly chosen principle of quiescence. The harmony of affairs has six items, the so-called six harmonies of reverence: 1. harmony of body in dwelling together, which is peaceful coexistence of the body; 2. harmony of speech in absence of dispute, which is speech that does not give rise to argument; 3. harmony of mind in shared joy, which is shared delight of mind and intention; 4. harmony of precepts in common cultivation, which is the common observance of precepts; 5. harmony of views in common understanding, which is complete agreement of views; 6. harmony of benefit in equal sharing, which is the equal sharing of benefits as one body. [The forbearance of the dharma of suffering] Amid the sufferings of the realm of desire, the mind of wisdom abides peacefully in the principle of true suchness. [The wisdom of the dharma of suffering] The undefiled wisdom obtained by contemplating the truth of suffering in the realm of desire. [The forbearance of the arising of dharmas] The various forbearances prior to the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas are called the forbearance of the arising of dharmas.
